notes.h: Role and the three headings of demand
notes.b: Every performer in a team or group activity has a job to do. To analyse that job, split what it asks of the performer into three separate headings: physical, personal and technical.
points: Role: a performer's specific position, function and responsibilities within an activity or team, such as goalkeeper, centre-back, point guard, setter in volleyball or lead dancer.

Physical demands: the fitness components a role relies on, such as endurance, power, agility, speed or reaction time. A midfielder, for example, needs cardio-respiratory endurance (heart and lungs supplying oxygen for long periods).

Personal demands: the psychological and interpersonal qualities (mental and people skills) a role needs, such as concentration, decision-making, communication, leadership, composure (staying calm), resilience (recovering from setbacks) and responsibility.

Technical demands: the skills and tactical knowledge a role needs to perform, such as a goalkeeper's handling and distribution, a point guard's ball-handling and passing, or a setter's volleying accuracy.
notes.tip: Keep the three headings separate. Fitness belongs under physical, never under personal, and examiners expect each demand placed under the right heading.

notes.b: The goalkeeper's role mixes explosive movement with concentration through long periods with little action.
points: Physical: power to dive and jump, agility to change direction quickly, and reaction time to a shot struck at close range, because there is almost no time to see the ball and respond.
Personal: concentration through long periods with little action, then sharp focus when a shot comes.
Personal: composure after conceding a goal, so one mistake does not lead to more, and leadership in directing the defensive line on positioning.
Technical: handling, meaning catching and holding the ball safely, and distribution, meaning throwing or kicking to team-mates to start attacks.
Technical: positioning, which reduces the angle and space the attacker can use to score.
notes.tip: If asked for demands on a role, name the role's specific need (for example reaction time to a close-range shot) rather than a general word like 'fitness'.

notes.b: The midfielder is involved in both attack and defence and needs endurance to cover ground across a whole game, so this role contrasts strongly with the goalkeeper.
points: Physical: high cardio-respiratory endurance to cover ground and repeat runs across a whole game, because the midfielder is involved in both attack and defence.
Physical: acceleration to win loose balls and reach space before an opponent.
Personal: decision-making about when to hold the ball, when to hand-pass and when to run into space.
Personal: resilience to keep working after a missed chance or a turnover (losing possession).
Technical: hand-passing and kicking accuracy under pressure from an opponent.
Technical: catching a high ball while an opponent is closing in.

notes.b: The point guard is the player who runs the team's attack, so quick thinking and control of the ball are key demands alongside speed.
points: Physical: speed and agility to get past defenders and to stay with fast opponents on defence.
Personal: decision-making in a fraction of a second about whether to pass, shoot or drive (run towards the basket).
Personal: leadership, because the point guard directs the team's offence and organises team-mates on the court.
Technical: ball-handling, meaning dribbling and protecting the ball under pressure.
Technical: passing to set up team-mates for scoring chances.
notes.tip: Questions ask for analysis of a named performer in a named activity. Give physical, personal and technical demands in turn, each with a reason tied to what the role does.

notes.h: Demands other than fitness: lead dancer
notes.b: Some questions tell you not to refer to fitness. Then you use only personal and technical demands, and a lead dancer shows how much a role can ask beyond fitness.
points: Personal: concentration to hold the sequence and its timing for the whole routine.
Personal: confidence to perform in front of an audience, so nerves do not spoil the performance.
Personal: responsibility to keep the group in time, because the other dancers follow the lead.
Technical: accurate execution of the choreographed movement (the planned steps), with clean body alignment and line.
Technical: learning the sequence quickly and performing it to the timing of the music.
notes.tip: When a question says you may not refer to fitness, identify a role and describe two demands, both personal or technical. Do not slip in endurance, power or other fitness components.

notes.b: A group performs better when its members feel they belong and work well together. Affiliation and team building are the ways a team creates that.
points: Affiliation: belonging to a team, club or group and identifying with it.
Formal affiliation to a club or governing body (the organisation that runs a sport) also gives access to competitions, insurance and coaching.
Team building develops trust, communication and cohesion (the bond that holds a group together) through shared goals, team activities and clear roles.
Task cohesion: team members working together towards a shared goal, such as winning a match.
Social cohesion: team members getting on well with one another, which makes working together easier.

notes.b: A captain or leader has influence over the whole group, so the way they behave can strengthen or damage the team.
points: A responsible captain or leader communicates clearly and sets an example in effort and behaviour, because team-mates copy what the leader does.
A responsible leader supports team-mates, keeps discipline and puts the team's goals before personal ones.
A leader who undermines the coach's plan or shows a poor attitude weakens the group, so responsible leaders support decisions even when they disagree with them.
notes.tip: Link each quality to its effect on the team, for example that setting an example in effort encourages others to match it.

notes.h: How clear roles and relationships improve performance
notes.b: When everyone knows their job and trusts their team-mates, players cover for each other and communicate well.
points: Players know their responsibilities, so every area of the pitch or court is covered and no two players chase the same task.
Players cover for each other when a team-mate is out of position or tired, so gaps do not stay open for the opposition.
Good communication lets players call for the ball, warn of an opponent and adjust during play.

notes.b: To exploit an opponent you first have to find where they are weak. Teams gather this information before a match and confirm it during play.
points: Scouting: watching the opponent in previous matches, live or on video.
Video analysis of previous matches shows patterns, such as where a defence leaves space or how a player reacts under pressure.
Notational statistics record how often a player or team uses a skill or position, so repeated patterns can be counted rather than guessed.
Early observation: watching the opening minutes of a game to confirm what scouting suggested.

notes.b: Weaknesses fall into four types: technical, physical, tactical and psychological. Each type is matched to a strategy that targets it. There is more on the strategies themselves in Structures, strategies and compositional elements.
points: Technical weakness (a flaw in a skill), such as a weak backhand or a weaker foot: direct serves, passes or shots to that side.
Physical weakness, such as slow defenders: play balls into the space behind them, where their lack of speed leaves them unable to recover.
Physical weakness, such as poor stamina late in a game: run at the tired defender late in the game.
Tactical weakness (a flaw in team organisation), such as a high defensive line: play balls into the space behind it.
Tactical weakness, such as poor marking at set pieces (planned restarts like corners and free kicks): attack set pieces with a planned routine that creates a free attacker.
Psychological weakness, such as losing composure under pressure: keep pressure on the player, forcing hurried decisions and errors.
notes.tip: A typical question asks you to identify two weaknesses an opposition team could have in a named activity and suggest a strategy to exploit one. Name the type of weakness and make the strategy match it.

keyTerms.definition: A performer's specific position, function and responsibilities within an activity or team.
The fitness components a role relies on, such as endurance, power, agility and speed.
The psychological and interpersonal qualities a role needs, such as concentration, communication and composure.
The skills and tactical knowledge a role needs to perform well.
Belonging to a team, club or group and identifying with it.
Developing trust, communication and cohesion within a group through shared goals, team activities and clear roles.
Team members working together towards a shared goal.
Team members getting on well with one another.
Leading a team by communicating clearly, setting an example, supporting team-mates and putting the team's goals first.
Watching an opponent in previous matches, live or on video, to find patterns and weaknesses.
Recording how often a player or team uses a skill, position or action so that patterns can be counted.
Using a strategy that targets a specific opponent weakness, such as a weak backhand or a slow defender.

factCards.definition: Physical (fitness components), personal (psychological and interpersonal), technical (skills and tactical knowledge).

factCards.term: Ways to identify an opponent's weaknesses
factCards.definition: Scouting, video analysis of previous matches, notational statistics and early observation.
Access to competitions, insurance and coaching.

questions.prompt: Analyse the physical, personal and technical demands of a performer role in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: soccer, centre-back. Physical demands: the role needs power to win aerial duels and jump to head the ball clear, and speed or agility to recover when an attacker runs in behind; a centre-back must also be able to repeat sprints across a match. Personal demands: concentration to track runners and hold the defensive line for the whole game; composure to stay calm after a mistake; and communication, directing team-mates on who marks whom at set pieces. Technical demands: heading accuracy to clear the ball or direct it to a team-mate; tackling and interceptions performed without giving away fouls; and the ability to pass out of defence under pressure. Each demand is needed because the centre-back is the last line of defence in the middle of the pitch, so a failure in any one of them leaves the goal exposed.

questions.prompt: Identify two weaknesses an opposing team could have and suggest a strategy to exploit one of them.
questions.model: Weakness 1: the opposing team defends with a high line and slow central defenders, so space opens behind them. Weakness 2: the team marks poorly at set pieces, leaving tall players unmarked near goal. Strategy to exploit the first weakness: play long balls and runs into the space behind the high line, so forwards with pace race onto the ball before the defenders can turn and recover.
